{{Short description|Power law growth of entropy of language or a stochastic process}}

'''Hilberg's hypothesis''' (also known as '''Hilberg's law''') is a conjecture in [[quantitative linguistics]] or a statistical law in [[information theory]]. It states that measures of information in [[natural language]] texts or samples of particular [[stochastic processes]] grow as a sublinear power of the sample length, possibly in addition to the term that is linear. It is closely related to [[Zipf's law]] and the [[neural scaling law]] for [[large language models]].

== Overview ==
Hilberg's hypothesis was proposed by the German telecommunication engineer [[Wolfgang Hilberg]]<ref>{{cite web | title=Wolfgang Hilberg (1932-2015) |url=https://www.tu-darmstadt.de/universitaet/organisation_verwaltung/geschichte_persoenlichkeiten/persoenlichkeiten_1/wolfgang_hilberg/index.en.jsp |access-date=25 March 2026}}</ref> in 1990,<ref name="Hilberg 1990">{{cite journal | last1=Hilberg | first1=Wolfgang | title=Der bekannte Grenzwert der redundanzfreien Information in Texten - eine Fehlinterpretation der Shannonschen Experimente? | journal=Frequenz | date=1990 | volume=44 | issue=9–10 | page=243 | doi=10.1515/FREQ.1990.44.9-10.243 | bibcode=1990Freq...44..243H | url=https://doi.org/10.1515/FREQ.1990.44.9-10.243 | url-access=subscription }}</ref> based on data originally published by [[Claude Shannon]] in 1951 on the predictability of English text.<ref name="Shannon 1951">{{cite journal | last1=Shannon | first1=Claude Elwood | title=Prediction and Entropy of Printed English | journal=Bell System Technical Journal | date=1951 | volume=30 | pages=50–64 | doi=10.1002/j.1538-7305.1951.tb01366.x | bibcode=1951BSTJ...30...50S | url=https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1951.tb01366.x | url-access=subscription }}</ref> Hilberg observed that the amount of new information per character appears to decrease with context length in a manner consistent with a [[power law]]. His analysis implied that the [[Shannon entropy]] <math>H(n)</math> of text blocks of length <math>n</math> grows approximately as
:<math>H(n)-hn \propto n^{\beta},</math>
where parameter <math>h</math> is the [[entropy rate]] of the process and parameter <math>\beta\in(0,1)</math> is called the Hilberg exponent.<ref name="Dębowski 2015">{{cite journal | last1=Dębowski | first1=Łukasz | title=Hilberg Exponents: New Measures of Long Memory in the Process | journal=IEEE Transactions on Information Theory | date=2015 | volume=61 | issue=10 | pages=5716–5726 | doi=10.1109/TIT.2015.2470675 | arxiv=1403.1757 | bibcode=2015ITIT...61.5716D | url=https://doi.org/10.1109/TIT.2015.2470675 }}</ref> The term proportional to <math>n^{\beta}</math> represents a memory effect, suggesting that human language carries a large amount of information in a repetitive way. Hilberg originally assumed that <math>h=0</math> and <math>\beta=1/2</math> basing his hypothesis on a visually meagre evidence.<ref name="Hilberg 1990"/> Hilberg's article was published in a local telecommunication journal and was initially noticed by physicists working in [[complex systems]].<ref name="Ebeling, Nicolis 1991">{{cite journal | last1=Ebeling | first1=W. | last2=Nicolis | first2=G. | title=Entropy of Symbolic Sequences: The Role of Correlations | journal=Europhysics Letters | date=1991 | volume=14 | issue=3 | pages=191–196 | doi=10.1209/0295-5075/14/3/001 | bibcode=1991EL.....14..191E | url=https://doi.org/10.1209/0295-5075/14/3/001 | url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name="Ebeling, Pöschel 1994">{{cite journal | last1=Ebeling | first1=W. | last2=Pöschel | first2=T. | title=Entropy and Long-Range Correlations in Literary English | journal=Europhysics Letters | date=1994 | volume=26 | issue=4 | pages=241–246 | doi=10.1209/0295-5075/26/4/001 | arxiv=cond-mat/0204108 | bibcode=1994EL.....26..241E | url=https://doi.org/10.1209/0295-5075/26/4/001 }}</ref><ref name="Bialek, Nemenman, Tishby 2001">{{cite journal | last1=Bialek | first1=William | last2=Nemenman | first2=Ilya | last3=Tishby | first3=Naftali | title=Predictability, Complexity, and Learning | journal=Neural Computation | date=2001 | volume=13 | issue=11 | pages=2409–2463 | doi=10.1162/089976601753195969 | pmid=11674845 | bibcode=2001NeCom..13.2409B | url=https://doi.org/10.1162/089976601753195969 | url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name="Crutchfield, Feldman 2003"/>

Hilberg's hypothesis implies that written or spoken language exhibits [[potential infinity|potentially infinite]] memory or [[long-range dependence|long-range statistical dependencies]] that cannot be captured by [[finite-state machine|finite-state]] [[hidden Markov models]]. The refutation of finite-state models based on Hilberg's hypothesis is close in spirit to [[Zipf's law]] for the unbounded [[arbitrariness|arbitrary]] lexicon, which needs to be learned and memorized by heart.<ref name="Dębowski 2021"/> This mechanism differs to the refutation of finite-state models that is based on the unbounded stack of the [[push-down automaton]] for processing [[syntax]] of natural language, the latter argument developed by [[Noam Chomsky]] in [[Syntactic Structures]] in 1957.

By contrast to "Hilberg's hypothesis", the term "Hilberg's law" or "Hilberg's condition" often applies to any [[stationary process]] that satisfies a power-law scaling of <math>H(n)-hn</math>.<ref name="Dębowski 2021"/> Quantity <math>H(n)</math> may represent various information measures, such as [[Shannon entropy]], (resource-bounded) [[Kolmogorov complexity]],<ref name="Achille, Soatto 2025">{{cite arXiv | last1=Achille | first1=Alessandro | last2=Soatto | first2=Stefano | title=AI Agents as Universal Task Solvers | date=2025 | class=cs.AI | eprint=2510.12066v1 }}</ref> or the length of a [[universal code (data compression)|universal code]].<ref name="Takahira et al. 2016">{{cite journal | last1=Takahira | first1=Ryosuke | last2=Tanaka-Ishii | first2=Kumiko | last3=Dębowski | first3=Łukasz | title=Entropy Rate Estimates for Natural Language—A New Extrapolation of Compressed Large-Scale Corpora | journal=Entropy | date=2016 | volume=18 | issue=10 | page=364 | doi=10.3390/e18100364 | doi-access=free }}</ref> In the context of [[deep learning]], the term [[neural scaling law]] is used for analogous power-law relations describing how performance of a [[large language model]], measured by [[cross entropy]], improves with data size, model parameters, or computation.<ref name="Kaplan et al. 2020">{{cite arXiv | last1=Kaplan | first1=Jared | last2=McCandlish | first2=Sam | last3=Henighan | first3=Tom | last4=Brown | first4=Tom B. | last5=Chess | first5=Benjamin | last6=Child | first6=Rewon | last7=Gray | first7=Scott | last8=Radford | first8=Alec | last9=Wu | first9=Jeffrey | last10=Amodei | first10=Dario | title=Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models | date=2020 | class=cs.LG | eprint=2001.08361 }}</ref> Yet another expression involves the [[mutual information]] between two adjacent text blocks of length <math>n</math>,
:<math>I(n) = 2H(n) - H(2n).</math>
Using this concept, Hilberg's law is equivalent to
:<math>I(n) \propto n^{\beta}.</math>
This version does not depend on the precise value of the entropy rate and is used in theoretical studies.<ref name="Dębowski 2021 b">{{cite book | last1=Dębowski | first1=Łukasz | title=Information Theory Meets Power Laws | publisher=Wiley | date=2020 | doi=10.1002/9781119625384 | isbn=978-1-119-62527-8 | url=https://doi.org/10.1002/9781119625384 }}</ref>

The value of the Hilberg exponent <math>\beta</math> depends crucially on the applied information measure, or the compression algorithm in case of the universal code. Simultaneously, it exhibits a certain degree of [[linguistic universal|universality]] across particular languages and writing systems, being
<math>\beta\approx 0.8</math> for the [[prediction by partial matching]] code run on English, French, Russian, Korean, Chinese, and Japanese news corpora.<ref name="Takahira et al. 2016"/><ref name="Tanaka-Ishii 2021">{{cite book | last1=Tanaka-Ishii | first1=Kumiko | title=Statistical Universals of Language | series=Mathematics in Mind | publisher=Springer | date=2021 | doi=10.1007/978-3-030-59377-3 | isbn=978-3-030-59376-6 | url=https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-59377-3 }}</ref>

== Examples of processes ==
The intuitive meaning of Hilberg's hypothesis can be motivated by some [[toy models]] of [[stationary process]]es, which link Hilberg's law with [[Zipf's law]] for an unbounded [[arbitrariness|arbitrary]] lexicon that needs to be learned by heart. Equivalently, the following examples may be considered as idealized information sources that convey an unbounded amount of [[algorithmically random]] knowledge in a repetitive fashion.<ref name="Dębowski 2021 b"/> This knowledge can be either immutable, giving rise to non-ergodic or perigraphic processes,<ref name="Dębowski 2011"/><ref name="Dębowski 2018"/> or slowly evolving, yielding mixing processes.<ref name="Dębowski 2012"/> A priori, this knowledge may encode also facts different to the knowledge of a particular lexicon.<ref name="Dębowski 2011"/>

A simple model of a stochastic process that satisfies Hilberg's law <math>I(n) \propto n^{\beta}</math> is given by the Santa Fe process. The Santa Fe process is a [[stationary ergodic process|stationary non-ergodic process]] <math>(X_i)_{i\in\mathbb{Z}}</math> that consists of pairs <math>X_i=(K_i,Z_{K_i})</math>, where <math>(K_i)_{i\in\mathbb{Z}}</math> is a sequence of independent random natural numbers distributed according to [[Zipf's law]] <math>P(K_i=k) \propto k^{-1/\beta}</math> and <math>(Z_k)_{k\in\mathbb{N}}</math> is the uniform [[Bernoulli process]], i.e., a sequence of fair coin flips.<ref name="Dębowski 2011">{{cite journal | last1=Dębowski | first1=Łukasz | title=On the Vocabulary of Grammar-Based Codes and the Logical Consistency of Texts | journal=IEEE Transactions on Information Theory | date=2011 | volume=57 | issue=7 | pages=4589–4599 | doi=10.1109/TIT.2011.2145170 | arxiv=0810.3125 | bibcode=2011ITIT...57.4589D | url=https://doi.org/10.1109/TIT.2011.2145170 }}</ref><ref name="Hutter 2021">{{cite arXiv | last1=Hutter | first1=Marcus | title=Learning Curve Theory | date=2021 | class=cs.LG | eprint=2102.04074 }}</ref> Process <math>(K_i)_{i\in\mathbb{Z}}</math> is called narration and process <math>(Z_k)_{k\in\mathbb{N}}</math> is called knowledge.<ref name="Dębowski 2021"/>
Individual variables <math>Z_k</math> are called (independent elementary) facts.<ref name="Dębowski 2011"/>

In general, Hilberg's law may arise for [[stationary ergodic process|non-ergodic]] or perigraphic processes depending whether one considers [[Shannon entropy]] or [[Kolmogorov complexity]] as the chosen information measure. A perigraphic process is roughly an [[algorithmically random]] [[ergodicity|ergodic component]] of a [[stationary ergodic process|non-ergodic]] process with a [[nonatomic measure|non-atomic]] [[invariant sigma-algebra]]. An example of a perigraphic process is a modified Santa Fe process <math>(X_i)_{i\in\mathbb{Z}}</math> that consists of pairs <math>X_i=(K_i,z_{K_i})</math> where <math>(z_k)_{k\in\mathbb{N}}</math> is a fixed [[algorithmically random]] binary sequence such as the [[halting probability]].<ref name="Dębowski 2018">{{cite journal | last1=Dębowski | first1=Łukasz | title=Is Natural Language a Perigraphic Process? The Theorem about Facts and Words Revisited | journal=Entropy | date=2018 | volume=20 | issue=2 | page=85 | doi=10.3390/e20020085 | pmid=33265176 | pmc=7512648 | arxiv=1706.04432 | bibcode=2018Entrp..20...85D | doi-access=free }}</ref>

Hilberg's law may also arise for some [[mixing (mathematics)|mixing processes]]. An example of such a process is a modified Santa Fe process <math>(X_i)_{i\in\mathbb{Z}}</math> that consists of pairs <math>X_i=(K_i,Z_{i,K_i})</math> where <math>(Z_{i,k})_{i\in\mathbb{Z},k\in\mathbb{N}}</math> is a collection of independent binary [[Markov process]]es, where the flipping probabilities <math>P(Z_{i,k}\neq Z_{i-1,k})</math> are smaller than the mentioning probabilities <math>P(K_i=k)</math>.<ref name="Dębowski 2012">{{cite journal | last1=Dębowski | first1=Łukasz | title=Mixing, Ergodic, and Nonergodic Processes with Rapidly Growing Information Between Blocks | journal=IEEE Transactions on Information Theory | date=2012 | volume=58 | issue=6 | pages=3392–3401 | doi=10.1109/TIT.2012.2190708 | arxiv=1103.3952 | bibcode=2012ITIT...58.3392D | url=https://doi.org/10.1109/TIT.2012.2190708 }}</ref>

The default examples of Santa Fe processes have a positive entropy rate. There are also examples of processes with a vanishing entropy rate that obey Hilberg's law, called multiperiodic processes.<ref name="Dębowski 2023">{{cite arXiv | last1=Dębowski | first1=Łukasz | title=Multiperiodic Processes: Ergodic Sources with a Sublinear Entropy | date=2023 | class=cs.IT | eprint=2302.09049 }}</ref>

== Related conditions ==
Hilberg's hypothesis connects quantitative linguistics, information theory, and modern machine-learning research on scaling behavior. By means of mathematical [[theorems]], Hilberg's law can be related to some similar conditions for [[stationary process]]es over a [[finite]], a [[countably infinite]], or an [[uncountable set]] of possible outcomes.

Hilberg's law can be deductively linked to  [[Zipf's law]] and [[Heaps' law]] for word-like subwords or chunks by means of [[grammar-based codes]] and [[prediction by partial matching]], [[stationary ergodic process|non-ergodic processes]], and the [[data-processing inequality]] for [[mutual information]].<ref name="Dębowski 2011"/><ref name="Dębowski 2018"/><ref name="Dębowski 2021 b"/> There is a general result concerning stationary processes, called the theorem about facts and words, which states that the mutual information between two adjacent text blocks is sandwiched by the number of independent elementary facts and the number of distinct word-like strings expressed in the concatenated text block.<ref name="Dębowski 2011"/><ref name="Dębowski 2018"/><ref name="Dębowski 2021 b"/>

Deductive links between Hilberg's law and the [[neural scaling law]] are a subject of ongoing research.<ref name="Hutter 2021"/><ref name="Achille, Soatto 2025"/><ref name="Dębowski 2025b">{{cite arXiv | last1=Dębowski | first1=Łukasz | title=From Zipf's Law to Neural Scaling through Heaps' Law and Hilberg's Hypothesis | date=2025 | class=cs.IT | eprint=2512.13491 }}</ref>

Hilberg's hypothesis has been discussed as evidence that language production involves infinite memory, contrasting with [[finite-state machine|finite-state]] [[Markov models]] and [[hidden Markov models]].<ref name="Dębowski 2021">{{cite journal | last1=Dębowski | first1=Łukasz | title=A Refutation of Finite-State Language Models through Zipf's Law for Factual Knowledge | journal=Entropy | date=2021 | volume=23 | issue=9 | page=1148 | doi=10.3390/e23091148 | pmid=34573773 | pmc=8465033 | bibcode=2021Entrp..23.1148D | doi-access=free }}</ref> In general, Hilberg's law is incompatible with [[finite-state machine|finite-state]] [[hidden Markov models]]. The mutual information between past and future <math>E=\lim_{n\to\infty} I(n)</math> is called [[excess entropy]]<ref name="Crutchfield, Feldman 2003"/> or [[predictive information]].<ref name="Bialek, Nemenman, Tishby 2001"/><ref name="Futrell, Hahn 2024">{{cite journal | last1=Futrell | first1=Richard | last2=Hahn | first2=Michael | title=Linguistic structure from a bottleneck on sequential information processing | journal=Nature Human Behaviour | date=2025 | doi=10.1038/s41562-025-02336-w | pmid=41286011 | doi-access=free }}</ref> Condition <math>E<\infty</math> holds for [[finite-state machine|finite-state]] [[hidden Markov models]]<ref name="Crutchfield, Feldman 2003">{{cite journal | last1=Crutchfield | first1=James P. | last2=Feldman | first2=David P. | title=Regularities unseen, randomness observed: Levels of entropy convergence | journal=Chaos: An Interdisciplinary Journal of Nonlinear Science | date=2003 | volume=13 | issue=1 | pages=25–54 | doi=10.1063/1.1530990 | pmid=12675408 | bibcode=2003Chaos..13...25C | url=https://doi.org/10.1063/1.1530990 | url-access=subscription }}</ref> and non-degenerate [[autoregressive moving-average model|autoregressive moving-average]] [[Gaussian processes]].<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Finch | first1=P. D. | title=On the Covariance Determinants of Moving-Average and Autoregressive Models | journal=Biometrika | date=1960 | volume=47 | issue=1/2 | pages=194–196 | doi=10.2307/2332974 | jstor=2332974 | doi-access=free }}</ref> By contrast, condition <math>E=\infty</math> holds for [[stationary ergodic process|non-ergodic processes]] with a [[nonatomic measure|non-atomic]] [[invariant sigma-algebra]].<ref name="Dębowski 2021 b"/> There also exist [[countably infinite]]-state [[hidden Markov models]] that enjoy condition <math>E=\infty</math><ref name="Travers, Cructhfield 2014">{{cite journal | last1=Travers | first1=Nicholas | last2=Crutchfield | first2=James | title=Infinite Excess Entropy Processes with Countable-State Generators | journal=Entropy | date=2014 | volume=16 | issue=3 | pages=1396–1413 | doi=10.3390/e16031396 | bibcode=2014Entrp..16.1396T | doi-access=free | arxiv=1111.3393 }}</ref> and Hilberg's law.<ref name="Dębowski 2014">{{cite journal | last1=Dębowski | first1=Łukasz | title=On Hidden Markov Processes with Infinite Excess Entropy | journal=Journal of Theoretical Probability | date=2014 | volume=27 | issue=2 | pages=539–551 | doi=10.1007/s10959-012-0468-6 | url=https://doi.org/10.1007/s10959-012-0468-6 | arxiv=1211.0834 }}</ref><ref name="Dębowski 2021"/>

A less direct is the link of Hilberg's law with the power-law logarithmic scaling of the maximal repetition length, empirically observed for natural language,<ref name="Dębowski 2015b">{{cite journal | last1=Dębowski | first1=Łukasz | title=Maximal Repetitions in Written Texts: Finite Energy Hypothesis vs. Strong Hilberg Conjecture | journal=Entropy | date=2015 | volume=17 | issue=8 | pages=5903–5919 | doi=10.3390/e17085903 | doi-access=free }}</ref> as this involves a power-law growth of [[Renyi entropies]] rather than the [[Shannon entropy]].<ref name="Dębowski 2025">{{cite journal | last1=Dębowski | first1=Łukasz | title=Repetition and recurrence times: Dual statements and summable mixing rates | journal=Electronic Communications in Probability | date=2025 | volume=30 | doi=10.1214/25-ECP718 | doi-access=free }}</ref>

In the case of stationary processes over a countable alphabet, it is unknown whether Hilberg's law (under a mild condition) implies a slow decay of the two-point mutual information <math>I(X_0;X_n)</math>, which seems to hold for natural language.<ref name="Lin, Tegmark 2017">{{cite journal | last1=Lin | first1=Henry | last2=Tegmark | first2=Max | title=Critical Behavior in Physics and Probabilistic Formal Languages | journal=Entropy | date=2017 | volume=19 | issue=7 | page=299 | doi=10.3390/e19070299 | arxiv=1606.06737 | bibcode=2017Entrp..19..299L | doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="Wieczyński, Dębowski 2025">{{cite journal | last1=Wieczyński | first1=Paweł | last2=Dębowski | first2=Łukasz | title=Long-Range Dependence in Word Time Series: The Cosine Correlation of Embeddings | journal=Entropy | date=2025 | volume=27 | issue=6 | page=613 | doi=10.3390/e27060613 | pmid=40566200 | pmc=12191972 | bibcode=2025Entrp..27..613W | doi-access=free }}</ref> For the non-ergodic Santa Fe processes, one also observes <math>I(X_0;X_n)=\text{const}</math> for <math>n\neq 0</math>.

In the case of [[real number|real-valued]] non-degenerate [[Gaussian processes]], condition <math>E=\infty</math> is equivalent to <math>\sum_{k=1}^\infty k\alpha_k^2=\infty</math>, where <math>\alpha_k</math> is the [[partial autocorrelation function]].<ref name="Dębowski 2007">{{cite journal | last1=Dębowski | first1=Łukasz | title=On processes with summable partial autocorrelations | journal=Statistics & Probability Letters | date=2007 | volume=77 | issue=7 | pages=752–759 | doi=10.1016/j.spl.2006.11.012 | url=https://doi.org/10.1016/j.spl.2006.11.012 }}</ref> Additionally, if the Gaussian process has a positive and continuous [[spectral density]] then condition <math>E=\infty</math> is equivalent to <math>\sum_{k=1}^\infty k\rho_k^2=\infty</math>, where <math>\rho_k</math> is the [[autocorrelation function]].<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Li | first1=Lei M. | title=Some Notes on Mutual Information Between Past and Future | journal=Journal of Time Series Analysis | date=2006 | volume=27 | issue=2 | pages=309–322 | doi=10.1111/j.1467-9892.2005.00469.x | url=https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-9892.2005.00469.x | url-access=subscription }}</ref> By contrast, the [[long-range dependence]] condition is <math>\sum_{k=1}^\infty |\rho_k|=\infty</math>,<ref>{{cite book | last1=Beran | first1=Jan | title=Statistics for Long-Memory Processes | date=2017 | doi=10.1201/9780203738481 | isbn=978-0-203-73848-1 | url=https://doi.org/10.1201/9780203738481 }}</ref> which is equivalent to the previous condition if the autocorrelation function <math>\rho_k</math> decays exactly according to a [[power law]]. Thus Hilberg's law implies [[long-range dependence]] if the process is Gaussian, the spectral density is positive and continuous, and the autocorrelation function follows a power law.
